objects: cross-population PRS; LD; allele frequencies; causal effects
assumptions: PRS trained in Europeans and applied to non-European populations
conclusion: European-trained PRS lose accuracy across populations, primarily because of LD, allele-frequency and causal-effect differences.
scope: Motivating setting; not a statement that the method removes all three sources.
span: However, many studies have shown that PRS based on European training data attain lower accuracy when applied to populations of non-European ancestry7–26. This loss of accuracy is primarily driven by LD differences12–15, allele frequency differences (including population-specific SNPs)13,14,27, and causal effect size differences12–14,28–31, though differences in heritability also play a minor role13,14,32.

objects: target genotype allele counts x_i; per-allele weights beta_i; predicted phenotype
conclusion: Prediction is a linear sum of allele counts multiplied by estimated per-allele effects.
scope: Prediction rule only; this passage does not specify a residual sampling likelihood.
span: All methods in this paper use a linear PRS, i.e., y ^ = ∑_{i} x_{i} β ^_{i}, where y ^ is the PRS of an individual, xi is the number of minor alleles of SNP i carried by that individual, and β ^_{i} is the estimated per-allele causal effect size of SNP i. The methods differ in the way they estimate β ^_{i}.

span: BOLT-LMM (resp. SBayesR) treats the effect of each SNP i as a random effect sampled from a mixture of two (resp. four) zero-mean normal distributions, whose variances and mixture weights are determined in a data-driven manner.

objects: target-cohort phenotypes; constituent PRSs; mixing weights
assumptions: training individuals from the target cohort
conclusion: Mixing weights are fitted by regressing target-cohort phenotypes on constituent PRSs using least squares constrained to nonnegative weights.
scope: Fitting procedure; size of the target training subset is a design choice.
span: PolyPred estimates the mixing weights via non-negative least squares estimation (i.e., least squares estimation constrained to produce to non-negative estimates) based on training individuals from the target cohort. Specifically, PolyPred (resp. PolyPred-S and PolyPred-P) estimates the mixing weights by computing the PRS corresponding to the PolyFun-pred effect sizes (given by y ^^{P o l y F u n – p r e d} = ∑_{i} x_{i} β ^_{i}^{P o l y F u n – p r e d}) and the PRS corresponding to the BOLT-LMM (resp. SBayesR and PRS-CS) PRSs.

span: The use of non-negative least squares estimation guarantees that the correlation of the predicted phenotype with the true phenotype is at least as large as the smallest of the correlations between each constituent predicted phenotype and the true phenotype.

objects: linear combination of PRSs; intercept; target-population bias
assumptions: combining PRSs instead of SNP effect estimates
conclusion: Combining PRSs permits an intercept that explicitly bias-corrects predictions to the target population.
scope: The authors describe PRS and SNP-weight combinations as almost mathematically identical.
span: In practice, we apply PolyPred and its summary statistic-based analogues by linearly combining the PolyFun-pred PRS and the BOLT-LMM (or SBayesR or PRS-CS) PRS (rather than linearly combining the SNP effect sizes). The two procedures are almost mathematically identical, with the only difference being that a linear combination of PRSs can also accommodate an intercept, which explicitly bias-corrects the PRS to the target population.

objects: overlapping loci; imputed SNPs; summary statistics; LD
assumptions: European training data; exclusions of HLA and two other long-range LD regions
conclusion: The implementation applies fine-mapping to overlapping 3Mb loci using BOLT-LMM summary statistics and summary LD, with ten causal SNPs per locus as the selected setting.
scope: Reported implementation uses 2763 loci, MAF above 0.1% and INFO above 0.6; ten effects and locus width are settings rather than assumptions.
span: Briefly, we applied PolyFun-pred across 2,763 overlapping 3Mb loci (equally spaced starting at chromosome 1, position 0) spanning 18,212,157 European MAF>0.1% imputed SNPs with INFO score>0.6 (excluding the HLA and two other long-range LD regions)35, assuming 10 causal SNPs per locus. We used summary statistics computed by BOLT-LMM, based on up to N=337,491 unrelated British-ancestry UK Biobank individuals, and using summary LD information estimated directly from the target samples.

objects: perfect causal effects; cross-population genetic correlation; allele-frequency differences
assumptions: even an infinite European training sample
conclusion: Perfectly estimated European causal effects can still leave a cross-population accuracy gap because genetic correlations may be below one and allele frequencies differ.
scope: Residual limitation even after addressing LD differences.
span: Even with an infinite European training sample, which allows estimating causal effects perfectly (thus addressing LD differences), prediction accuracy could still be higher for Europeans vs. non-Europeans due to cross-population genetic correlations less than 113,30,63,64 and different allele frequencies (including population-specific SNPs) (Supplementary Note).
